For claim c1:
GOV.UK published on May 6, 2020, states there is no evidence linking 5G and coronavirus, and that viruses cannot travel on radio waves or mobile networks. It also notes that coronavirus is spreading in countries without 5G. [1] The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a UN agency, confirmed on April 22, 2020, that the theory of a link between 5G and COVID-19 is "a hoax that has no technical basis." [2] The World Health Organization (WHO) and Centers for Disease Control (CDC) state that viruses cannot travel via radio waves or mobile networks, and that physical contact is needed for infection. [3] [4] [5] Wikipedia, citing the CDC, explains that 5G uses non-ionizing radiation which does not damage DNA, and there is no evidence that it affects the immune system. [6]

For claim c2:
AP News reported on April 8, 2020, that claims of maps showing a correlation between confirmed COVID-19 cases and 5G installation are false. The article explains that both maps simply highlight densely populated areas, and that 5G is typically rolled out in urban centers where population density is higher. [7] A study published in Medical Research Archives on April 12, 2021, found a statistical correlation between higher COVID-19 cases and deaths in US states and counties with 5G millimeter wave wireless telecommunications, even after accounting for population density. [8] However, this study does not claim causation, and other sources strongly refute any causal link. [7] [9] [10] The Guardian reported on April 7, 2020, that a popular claim about Wuhan being the first city to receive 5G and the origin of COVID-19 is false, as other cities had 5G earlier, and countries without 5G also experienced high numbers of cases. [11] UNICEF Montenegro stated on July 12, 2021, that their analysis shows 5G does not spread coronavirus. [12]
